blocks.prompt: The Coat That Keeps Growing
blocks.text: A sheep wears a coat it can never take off. The coat is made of wool, and it grows all year long. It grows in summer. It grows in winter. It never stops. Once a year the farmer shears the sheep. Sharp clippers cut the wool off in one big piece. The sheep does not feel it. The wool is soft and warm, and people spin it into yarn for socks and hats. Then the sheep starts growing a new coat. Sheep eat grass all day. They stay in a flock so no one gets left alone.

blocks.prompt: The Coat That Cannot Fall Off
blocks.text: Wild sheep do not need haircuts. A wild sheep grows a warm coat for winter, and when spring comes, the coat falls out on its own. The sheep rubs against a rock, the old wool drops off, and that is that. Farm sheep cannot do this. For thousands of years, people picked the sheep with the thickest wool and bred more sheep like them. Little by little, the shedding stopped. Today most farm sheep grow wool all year and never let it go. They need people to cut it off. A sheep in New Zealand named Shrek proved what happens if nobody does. Shrek ran away and hid in a cave for six years. When he was finally found, he was a giant ball of wool. His fleece weighed about sixty pounds. That is enough wool for twenty suits. Shrek could barely see. Once he was shorn, he looked like a sheep again, and he seemed much happier about it.

blocks.prompt: The Animal That Can See Behind Itself
blocks.text: Look closely at a sheep's eye and you will see something odd. The pupil is not a circle. It is a wide black rectangle lying on its side, like a letter box. That shape is not an accident. A sheep is a prey animal. It spends its day with its head down in the grass, and the whole time it needs to know what is sneaking up behind it. The rectangular pupil works like a panoramic window. It lets in light from a wide strip of the world and blurs out the sky above and the dirt below, which a sheep does not need to watch. With eyes set on the sides of its head, a sheep can see almost all the way around itself, roughly three hundred degrees, without moving its head at all. There is a stranger part. When a sheep lowers its head to graze, its eyes rotate in their sockets to keep those rectangles level with the horizon. The head tips down. The pupils stay flat. The panorama never tilts. Sheep are also better at recognizing faces than most people expect. In one experiment, sheep learned to tell fifty other sheep apart from photographs and still remembered them two years later. The animal we use as a symbol of mindless following is quietly keeping track of everyone in the flock.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Wool is keratin, like your fingernails

blocks.prompt: Wool Is a Solved Problem
blocks.text: Wool is the strangest thing a farm produces, because it is not really a product at all. It is a solved problem. Start with the fiber. A single strand of wool is made of keratin, the same protein in your fingernails, but it does not grow straight. It grows in a wave, a natural spring called crimp. Merino wool can crimp as many as a hundred times in a single inch. Pack millions of those springs together and they cannot lie flat. They hold each other apart, and the gaps fill with still air. That trapped air, not the fiber, is what keeps a sheep warm on a freezing hillside. Wool is mostly nothing, arranged carefully. Then there is water. Every wool fiber is coated in lanolin, a waxy grease the sheep makes in its own skin, and rain rolls off it. But the inside of the fiber does the opposite: it drinks. Wool can take on about a third of its own weight in moisture before it feels wet to the touch, and as it absorbs water it releases a small amount of heat. A wet sheep in a cold wind is doing better than it looks. Wool is also very hard to burn. It holds water and nitrogen, it needs more oxygen to stay alight than the air around it contains, and when the flame leaves, it goes out. This is why wool ends up in airplane seats and firefighters' clothing long after cheaper fibers were available. None of this was designed in a laboratory. It was assembled by evolution on wild sheep in cold mountains, and then pushed much further by ten thousand years of humans choosing which sheep got to have lambs. We did not invent wool. We just kept turning up the volume on it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Ovis aries, bred from the wild mouflon
Domesticated about 11,000 years ago
Woolly fleeces appear about 6,000 years ago
Dolly the sheep was cloned in 1996
The Woolsack still sits in the House of Lords
Over a billion sheep alive today

blocks.prompt: The Animal We Redesigned
blocks.text: There is a wild sheep still living in the mountains of western Asia. It is called the mouflon. It is lean and quick, it has curling horns, and its coat is short, coarse hair over a thin layer of soft fluff. In spring, that fluff falls out on its own. If you met a mouflon on a hillside, you would not think of a sweater. Every domestic sheep alive descends from an animal like that. Around eleven thousand years ago, in the hills of the Fertile Crescent, people began keeping mouflon instead of hunting them. The first flocks were not kept for wool. They were kept for meat, milk, and skins, and for several thousand years the sheep in those pens looked much like the sheep on the mountain. Then something slow and enormous happened. People noticed that a few animals carried more of the soft undercoat than the coarse outer hair, and that a few of those animals were slower to shed it. Those were the sheep that were allowed to breed. Repeat that choice for a hundred generations, then a thousand, and the undercoat takes over the whole animal. By around six thousand years ago, sheep with true woolly fleeces appear in the archaeological record. The shedding had been bred out. The haircut had been bred in. Consider what that means. A modern Merino cannot survive without us. Left alone, its fleece keeps growing until the animal overheats, cannot move well, and cannot escape. We did not domesticate a woolly animal. We built one, and in building it we made it permanently dependent on the species that built it. The wool paid us back. Medieval England ran on it. Wool taxes funded wars, wool merchants funded cathedrals, and to this day the presiding officer of the House of Lords sits on the Woolsack, a large cushion stuffed with wool, placed there in the fourteenth century so that nobody in government could forget where the money came from. The sheep has stayed at the center of our experiments ever since. In 1996, at the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh, a lamb was born who had no father and whose genetic instructions came from a single udder cell taken from a six year old ewe. Her name was Dolly, and she was the first mammal cloned from an adult body cell. The animal chosen for the most radical biological experiment of the century was, once again, a sheep. Eleven thousand years in, we are still editing the same animal. What we have never done is finish.
